article.title: Second nature

items.sentence_raw: Psychologists have long held that a person's character cannot undergo a transformation in any meaningful way and that the key traits of personality are determined at a very young age.
items.explain:
Q14: The passage says psychologists believed a person's character cannot undergo a *'transformation'* — **'transformation'** means a big **change**. So the answer is **transformation** or **change**.

Q15: The passage says personality traits are determined at a *'very young age'* — this means when you are very little. So the answer is **young age**.

items.sentence_raw: However, researchers have begun looking more closely at ways we can change.
Positive psychologists have identified 24 qualities we admire, such as loyalty and kindness, and are studying them to find out why they come so naturally to some people.
What they're discovering is that many of these qualities amount to habitual behaviour that determines the way we respond to the world.
The good news is that all this can be learned.
Some qualities are less challenging to develop than others, optimism being one of them.
items.explain: Q16: The passage says some qualities are less challenging to develop, *'optimism being one of them'* — **'less challenging'** means easier. So the easiest quality to acquire is **optimism**.

items.sentence_raw: However, developing qualities requires mastering a range of skills which are diverse and sometimes surprising.
items.explain: Q17: The passage says developing qualities requires mastering a range of *'skills'* — **'mastering'** means learning, and **'a range of'** means a wide variety. So the answer is **skills** or **techniques**.

items.sentence_raw: For example, to bring more joy and passion into your life, you must be open to experiencing negative emotions.
items.explain: Q18: The passage says to bring more joy, you must be open to experiencing *'negative emotions'* — **'joy'** means happiness, and **'experiencing'** means feeling. So the answer is **negative emotions** or **negative feelings**.

items.sentence_raw: Cultivating such qualities will help you realise your full potential.
"The evidence is good that most personality traits can be altered," says Christopher Peterson, professor of psychology at the University of Michigan, who cites himself as an example.
Inherently introverted, he realised early on that as an academic, his reticence would prove disastrous in the lecture hall.
items.explain: Q22: The question says it is possible to overcome shyness to speak in public. Christopher Peterson was *'inherently introverted'* — **'introverted'** means shy — but he learned to be *'more outgoing'* for the lecture hall. So the answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: So he learned to be more outgoing and to entertain his classes.
items.explain: Q22: The question says it is possible to overcome shyness to speak in public. Christopher Peterson was *'inherently introverted'* — **'introverted'** means shy — but he learned to be *'more outgoing'* for the lecture hall. So the answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: "Now my extroverted behaviour is spontaneous," he says.
David Fajgenbaum had to make a similar transition.
He was preparing for university, when he had an accident that put an end to his sports career.
On campus, he quickly found that beyond ordinary counselling, the university had no services for students who were undergoing physical rehabilitation and suffering from depression like him.
items.explain: Q24: The question asks how someone overcame a sad experience. David Fajgenbaum was *'suffering from depression'* after an accident — **'depression'** is a sad experience — but he launched a support group to help others. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: He therefore launched a support group to help others in similar situations.
items.explain: Q24: The question asks how someone overcame a sad experience. David Fajgenbaum was *'suffering from depression'* after an accident — **'depression'** is a sad experience — but he launched a support group to help others. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: He took action despite his own pain - a typical response of an optimist.
Suzanne Segerstrom, professor of psychology at the University of Kentucky, believes that the key to increasing optimism is through cultivating optimistic behaviour, rather than positive thinking.
She recommends you train yourself to pay attention to good fortune by writing down three positive things that come about each day.
items.explain: Q20: The question says people should actively notice good things. Suzanne Segerstrom recommends you *'pay attention to good fortune'* — **'pay attention to'** means actively notice, and **'good fortune'** means good things. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: This will help you convince yourself that favourable outcomes actually happen all the time, making it easier to begin taking action.
You can recognise a person who is passionate about a pursuit by the way they are so strongly involved in it.
Tanya Streeter's passion is freediving - the sport of plunging deep into the water without tanks or other breathing equipment.
Beginning in 1998, she set nine world records and can hold her breath for six minutes.
The physical stamina required for this sport is intense but the psychological demands are even more overwhelming.
Streeter learned to untangle her fears from her judgment of what her body and mind could do.
items.explain: Q23: The question asks about rational thinking helping someone achieve physical goals. Tanya Streeter learned to *'untangle her fears from her judgment'* — **'judgment'** means rational thinking, and this helped her in freediving, a physical sport. So the answer is **E**.

items.sentence_raw: "In my career as a competitive freediver, there was a limit to what I could do - but it wasn't anywhere near what I thought it was," she says.
Finding a pursuit that excites you can improve anyone's life.

The secret about consuming passions, though, according to psychologist Paul Silvia of the University of North Carolina, is that "they require discipline, hard work and ability, which is why they are so rewarding."
Psychologist Todd Kashdan has this advice for those people taking up a new passion: "As a newcomer, you also have to tolerate and laugh at your own ignorance.
items.explain: Q19: The question says people must accept they do not know much when trying something new. Todd Kashdan says a newcomer must *'tolerate and laugh at your own ignorance'* — **'ignorance'** means not knowing much. So the answer is **E**.

items.sentence_raw: You must be willing to accept the negative feelings that come your way," he says.
In 2004, physician-scientist Mauro Zappaterra began his PhD research at Harvard Medical School.
Unfortunately, he was miserable as his research wasn't compatible with his curiosity about healing.
items.explain: Q25: The question asks about someone rethinking their academic career path. Mauro Zappaterra was miserable in his PhD research, so he took a break, learned new things, and then *'switched labs'* — **'switched'** means he changed his path. So the answer is **G**.

items.sentence_raw: He finally took a break and during eight months in Santa Fe, Zappaterra learned about alternative healing techniques not taught at Harvard.
items.explain: Q25: The question asks about someone rethinking their academic career path. Mauro Zappaterra was miserable in his PhD research, so he took a break, learned new things, and then *'switched labs'* — **'switched'** means he changed his path. So the answer is **G**.

items.sentence_raw: When he got back, he switched labs to study how cerebrospinal fluid nourishes the developing nervous system.
items.explain: Q25: The question asks about someone rethinking their academic career path. Mauro Zappaterra was miserable in his PhD research, so he took a break, learned new things, and then *'switched labs'* — **'switched'** means he changed his path. So the answer is **G**.

items.sentence_raw: He also vowed to look for the joy in everything, including failure, as this could help him learn about his research and himself.
One thing that can hold joy back is a person's concentration on avoiding failure rather than their looking forward to doing something well.
"Focusing on being safe might get in the way of your reaching your goals," explains Kashdan.
For example, are you hoping to get through a business lunch without embarrassing yourself, or are you thinking about how fascinating the conversation might be?
Usually, we think of courage in physical terms but ordinary life demands something else.
For marketing executive Kenneth Pedeleose, it meant speaking out against something he thought was ethically wrong.
items.explain: Q26: The question asks about someone risking his career out of duty. Kenneth Pedeleose spoke out against something *'ethically wrong'* — **'ethically wrong'** means against his sense of duty — knowing his *'job security would be threatened'*. So the answer is **H**.

items.sentence_raw: The new manager was intimidating staff so Pedeleose carefully recorded each instance of bullying and eventually took the evidence to a senior director, knowing his own job security would be threatened.
items.explain: Q26: The question asks about someone risking his career out of duty. Kenneth Pedeleose spoke out against something *'ethically wrong'* — **'ethically wrong'** means against his sense of duty — knowing his *'job security would be threatened'*. So the answer is **H**.

items.sentence_raw: Eventually the manager was the one to go.
According to Cynthia Pury, a psychologist at Clemson University, Pedeleose's story proves the point that courage is not motivated by fearlessness, but by moral obligation.
items.explain: Q21: The question says courage can be learned once its origins in responsibility are understood. Cynthia Pury says courage is motivated by *'moral obligation'* — **'moral obligation'** means a sense of responsibility. So the answer is **G**.

items.sentence_raw: Pury also believes that people can acquire courage.

Many of her students said that faced with a risky situation, they first tried to calm themselves down, then looked for a way to mitigate the danger, just as Pedeleose did by documenting his allegations.
Over the long term, picking up a new character trait may help you move toward being the person you want to be.
And in the short term, the effort itself could be surprisingly rewarding, a kind of internal adventure.

subtitles: Your personality isn't necessarily set in stone. With a little experimentation, people can reshape their temperaments and inject passion, optimism, joy and courage into their lives
